speechtext:
I believe it is important for the municipalities to give more consideration to this housing problem. I referred a moment ago to the building bylaws as an illustration of that. Apparently it is necessary for some people to build in the cities where sewers and other facilities are available. I should like to suggest to the people of this country

that they might be well advised to build outside the cities where they would not find such high taxation. It is true they would have to do without sewers, sidewalks, pavements and that sort of thing, but those are the factors which add to the cost of owning a house in the city.
In northern Ontario there are two town-sites upon which fine houses have been built at surprisingly low cost. Approximately four or five thousand five-room houses have been built of aluminum. I cannot see why the cost could not be lowered if research were conducted into construction methods. There are plenty of capable engineers, and I believe research should be encouraged. If such research were conducted, it should be remembered that it must be conducted by the government. I believe there is an appropriation of approximately $5 million to be expended over a five-year period for that purpose. I understand the government has spent $1 million of that. This is one method by which the government could contribute a great deal to so many people. I believe it would be well advised to seriously consider further research work. This framing to which I referred a few moments ago could be done in the factories.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I hope some of the observations I have made will be considered by the government. I mention them because house building has been carried on mainly by private enterprise. If we look over the records of the cost of administration of government projects, I believe they will verify the fact that the government would like to be absolved of all responsibility for housing. For that reason,
I hope some of the suggestions and comments I have made will be considered.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, rising in this debate I should like to tell the new members of this house something of our province. Many of the new members have not visited Prince Edward Island, so I should like to extend an invitation to them to visit the province and learn for themselves about its scenic beauty.
As you know, Prince Edward Island is located in the gulf of St. Lawrence, with Northumberland strait dividing it from the mainland. There are two ferry services, one crossing from Port Borden, Prince Edward Island, to Tormentine, New Brunswick. The boat on this service is said to be the largest icebreaker in the world. It is capable of carrying approximately nineteen railway cars and about sixty automobiles and trucks. The second service is from Cariboo, Nova Scotia, to Wood Island, Prince Edward Island. This ferry service carries passengers and motor vehicles only. Last year a bus service was
The Budget-Mr. Kickham inaugurated from Moncton to Charlottetown, which greatly assists in speeding up passenger traffic from Moncton. Hon. members are probably aware of the fact that there is also an air service from the United States and Canadian points to Charlottetown.
The main interests in Prince Edward Island are farming, fishing and the tourist business. Potatoes are our main cash crop. Prince Edward Island seed potatoes are known the world over. We have shipped them to Argentina, British West Indies, Cuba, France, Mexico, Newfoundland, Palestine, Egypt, Panama, South Africa, and the United States. We supply over 55 per cent of the Canadian requirements for certified seed. Many of the markets I have named are not available to us now. These were markets emanating out of war conditions. We must now depend largely on the United States and Canada for our markets.
Two years ago our provincial government passed an act known as the Potato Act, compelling all growers to plant certified seed or better. The highest grade is known as foundation. So that our seed is practically disease-free, coming as it does from what we strive to make a disease-free area.
Our shipments to the United States are subject to a regular duty of 75 cents per hundredweight. This government, however, obtained for us from the United States government a quota for 3,500,000 bushels at the reduced rate of 37 i cents per hundredweight. While we appreciate this fact, we should like to see the quota increased by another 2 million bushels. If this could be arranged, it would assist in offsetting the adverse balance of trade between Canada and the United States.
Last marketing season the government gave us a floor price of $1.15 per hundredweight; this action had a beneficial effect in stabilizing the marketing of the crop. We are faced again this year with the same conditions as those that obtained last season, and we hope and trust that this government will do for us what they did last season, thereby preventing serious financial loss to the growers. It could well be that no loss would be suffered by this government owing to the greatly reduced crop in the United States and Canada. The estimated production in the United States for 1949 is 378,805,000 bushels, which is 67,045,000 less than last year. The estimate for Canada in 1949 is
82,745,000	bushels, which is 9,355,000 bushels less than last year, making a total decrease in the United States and Canada of 76,400,000 bushels. The total consumption in Canada and the United States is approximately 480 million bushels, so that this year's production is 18,450,000 bushels under normal

The Budget-Mr. Kickham requirements. A great advantage would accrue from having the support price in effect as early as possible, thus preventing panicky marketing and assuring the growers of something near the cost of production.
The recently increased freight rate of 29 cents per hundredweight is a serious handicap to our potato industry. Before the first increase in 1948 of 21 per cent, our rate to Toronto, for example, was 39 cents per hundredweight; now it is 51 cents, or 30 cents per bushel. In all, it costs around $290 to ship a car of potatoes to Toronto, including freight, "reefer" charges and heat en route.
The provinces of Quebec and Ontario should be as much interested in the potato industry in our province as we are ourselves. Why is this so? The reason is that we buy from central Canada approximately $24 million worth of all commodities each year. Not only is the money which we receive from Quebec and Ontario returned to them for goods of every description that we need, but all the dollars that we receive from sales outside Canada, particularly from the United States, are spent by us in central Canada, thereby greatly assisting in keeping their wheels of industry revolving.
Furthermore, were it not for the fact that our potatoes receive a premium on those markets, earned because of their quality, we could not compete with Quebec and Ontario-grown potatoes, because of their nearness to the consuming centres in those provinces where, by rail and trucks, they can be delivered for a fraction of our costs.
Potatoes are our cash crop, in the same way as wheat is the cash crop for the western farmer. Our government provides the wheat grower with a support price; we feel that we are also entitled to a support price, and that it would be of as much advantage to central Canada as to our province. Again, if our potato industry is ruined by exorbitant freight rates that apply,-and that are as effective as high tariffs,-between the provinces, the Canadian National Railways will suffer equally. I cannot see why we should be penalized because of our geographical location in Canada in relation to other provinces with whom we must do business, and because of existing tariff regulations between Canada and the United States.
I wish to tender this solution of the problem to the government. Rather than increase our freight rates, should any loss be sustained by the government the loss should be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund, thereby encouraging free exchange of commodities between the provinces.
Our second largest industry is fishing. The principal varieties of fish are lobsters, cod, hake, mackerel, herring, clams and oysters.

Because of the quality of our lobsters, we have no difficulty in finding markets in Canada and the United States. Our big problem now is to find profitable markets for salted, dried fish. During and immediately following the war, our total catch of cod and hake was canned, purchased by UNRRA and shipped to Europe. This market is not now available.
In the discussion on the second reading of the Fish Inspection Act, I noticed that members stressed the importance of putting up a high grade and quality of fish. We have a problem in my constituency in this respect, as many of our harbours are too shoal for the boats to reach the dressing stands at low tide. As a result, the boats must wait outside until the tide rises, while the fisherman covers his catch from the hot sun. Nevertheless, the quicker the fish are split and salted, the better the grade that will be procured.
This is a matter for both the Department of Fisheries and the Department of Public Works. I bring this problem to the attention of both departments, trusting that those conditions I have mentioned will now be remedied. In the past the answer has been that no steel, cement or lumber were available to extend the work at those harbours and also that there was a shortage of dredging equipment. I do not think that those answers are good enough now.
Our third industry is our tourist business which brings in approximately $2,800,000 each year. I do not wish to take up too much time of the house but, before taking my seat, I want to say that having regard to the remuneration received by teachers in other provinces our teachers in Prince Edward Island receive the least. Why is this? Because of our people having the lowest income per capita of any province in Canada; and this is because of our geographical disadvantages, as I have tried to point out to this house. For example, the personal income per capita in Prince Edward Island is $548; Nova Scotia, $682; New Brunswick, $636; Quebec, $784; Ontario $1,075; Manitoba, $946; Alberta, $998 and British Columbia, $1,024. The other provinces of Canada receive the benefits of the education and of the talents of most of those who receive a good education in Prince Edward Island. Our population was 105,000 when we joined confederation in 1873; now I believe it is 93,000. As the smallest province of Canada we are entitled to greater consideration and to be given the measure of equality which is due to all Canadians.
Before taking my seat I wish to support what was said by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Riley) endorsing the Chig-necto canal.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is the house ready for the question?
Amendment negatived.
Main motion (Mr. Abbott) agreed to on division.

The house in committee of ways and means, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
Resolved that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Excise Tax Act and to provide:
1.	That the following excise taxes be repealed, namely, the excise taxes on: (a) soft drinks; (b) chocolate, candy, and confectionery; (c) chewing gum; (d) cable, telegraph, and telephone messages, and on telephone extensions; (e) transportation tickets or rights of transportation, and on seats, berths, or other sleeping accommodation; (f) motor buses; and (g) carbonic acid gas.
2.	That the retail purchase tax be repealed and replaced by an excise tax of 10 per cent, payable by the manufacturer or importer, on all articles now subject to the retail purchase tax.
3.	That the following excise taxes be reduced from 35 per cent to 10 per cent, namely, the excise taxes on: (a) trunks, suitcases, bags, and luggage of all kinds; (b) ash trays, tobacco pipes, and smokers' accessories; and (c) fountain pens, propelling pencils, and desk accessories.
4.	That the following excise taxes be reduced from 25 per cent to 10 per cent, namely, the excise taxes on: (a) toilet articles; (b) devices commonly or commercially known as lighters; and (c) coin, disc, or token operated machines and vending machines.
5.	That the sales tax on the following articles be repealed: lactose; malt syrup except when sold for beverage purposes; diesel powered self-propelled trucks, mounted on rubber tired wheels, for off highway use exclusively at mines and quarries, and complete parts thereof.
6.	That the rates of excise tax on matches be amended from the present specific proportionate rate of tax on each package, to an ad valorem tax of 10 per cent.
7.	That the present specific tax of 5 cents per pound on tires and tubes be amended to an ad valorem tax of 10 per cent.
8.	That the sales tax on the following articles be repealed: liquid fuel for lighting or heating, but not including fuel when for use in internal combustion engines; crude oil to be used for the production of fuel.
9.	That the excise tax on wines containing not more than 7 per cent of proof spirit be reduced from 50 cents per gallon to 25 cents per gallon.
10.	That paragraphs 1 to 7 shall have effect on and after March 23, 1949, and paragraphs 8 and 9 shall have effect on and after October 21, 1949.

speakeroldname: Mr. James Sinclair (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution to amend the Excise Tax Act is just one resolution but for the convenience of hon. members it is broken down into its various subheadings. For the benefit of the new members perhaps I should make just a brief explanation of the purpose of the tax reductions. For the most part, these tax reductions occurred in the budget which was presented in the spring by the Minister of
Excise Tax Act
Finance (Mr. Abbott) and were repeated, with two extensions, in the budget delivered in October. While hon. members will welcome any tax reduction, this resolution, with its various parts, provides for actually more than tax reductions because there is a measure which may be called a tidying-up job done in the entire excise tax structure of Canada.
Our indirect tax structure now falls into four main groups. The first group is a large group of commodities on which there is no sales tax nor excise tax. They are the commodities which are covered in schedule III of the Excise Tax Act. I am quite sure that if hon. members would refer to that list they would be amazed at the number of commodities in this country on which neither sales tax nor excise tax is levied.
Federal sales tax.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member will appreciate that these excise taxes and sales taxes are federal taxes.
Will the hon. member put them on the record?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: They are already on record as schedule III of the Excise Tax Act.
I understand that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If there is any desire to have schedule III placed on record that could be done.
Agreed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I think it would be very helpful to hon. members in the study of these questions to place them on Hansard.
The next group is a group on which sales tax is levied. That is actually schedule II of the Excise Tax Act. It also will be placed on Hansard.
Then the third group in the old Excise Tax Act was varied in taxation structure. We had a variety of taxes, namely, 15 per cent, 25 per cent, 35 per cent at various levels, the manufacturers' level and the retail level. I know it was confusing to the public and also difficult to administer as far as the department was concerned. Therefore the major tidying-up job which has been done is in this third group. The excise taxes have all been reduced to 10 per cent at the manufacturers' level.
Then, there is the fourth group, in which no change has been made, namely, the excise duties on which traditionally high taxes on tobacco and liquor, which are regarded in the luxury class, have been levied. Therefore we have four classes in our excise tax structure. The first class is foodstuffs and building materials, on which there is neither federal sales tax nor excise tax. Then there

Excise Tax Act
is the second group of quite essential commodities on which the 8 per cent sales tax is levied. Next is the third group on which in addition a 10 per cent excise tax is levied; and finally the fourth group, tobacco and liquor, on which our traditionally high excise duties are levied.
I would suggest that it would be best to have the committee study the various subheadings.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall we adopt the resolution?
Resolution agreed to.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think only resolution 1 has been carried.
May we take each section in turn?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Yes. Section 1 of the resolution has been discussed and I understand that it has been agreed to. We shall now proceed with section 2.
2. That the retail purchase tax be repealed and replaced by an excise tax ot 10 per cent, payable by the manufacturer or importer, on all articles now subject to the retail purchase tax.
Watches would come under this resolution?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes.
This resolution deals with the luxury tax which used to be 25 per cent and has now been reduced to 10 per cent?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes.
I protest against the tax still being on watches and clocks because they are not luxuries. I feel the tax should be taken off watches and clocks because they are a necessity.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: This resolution covers pretty well the 25 per cent tax which was placed on things handled by jewelers. It included watches and clocks over a certain price range. This is not a luxury tax. During wartime it was placed on the retail level not so much for its revenue-raising potential but rather to discourage the buying of what were regarded as articles not absolutely essential for war needs. As hon. members know, it was very successful in discouraging purchases from jewelers and this was one of the main reasons why the jewelers of Canada protested very strongly against the continuance of this tax. This improvement has been brought down by reducing the tax from 25 per cent at the retail level to 10 per cent on the wholesale value.
What is the value of the clock or watch which is not now taxed? What is the range?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I must confess that it slips my mind at the moment. It is quite low, around $5. I shall bring that information in later.
The resolution should stand.

In connection with this section 2, let me say I am definitely opposed to the principle of converting what was an ultimate purchasers' tax into what will now be a hidden sales tax imposed at the manufacturer's level. The main purpose, evidently, is to bring the taxes on the items covered by section 2 into line with the general sales tax provisions-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Excise tax.

Excise tax or sales tax, it does not matter much; the principle is the same. It becomes a hidden tax added on at the manufacturer's level. We have pointed out repeatedly that we are opposed to this type of taxation, for the main reason that it sets in motion a vicious spiral of increased cost to the consumer. On the general principle, and with complete disregard for the items mentioned, we do wish to protest. We feel the people of this country are entitled to know what fraction or part of the cost of an article they are buying is in reality taxation and what fraction or part is in reality cost.
We feel that the responsibility for imposing taxes ought to rest with the government of the day. How else can the people of this country know what the taxes really are? I believe hon. members who have considered this matter carefully will agree that the best barometer by which to judge the efficiency of government is the level of taxation imposed upon the people. Until the people have a fair chance to see the barometer, and to keep it ever in front of them, so that they can measure the efficiency of the government, there can be no gauge or standard by which they can tell whether or not the government is efficient.
Under the circumstances we of the Social Credit party protest strongly against this move to add one more hidden tax to the great burden of taxation borne by the Canadian people today and, sir, which in the main is responsible for pushing up the cost of living by, I submit, fully 20 or 25 per cent.
The parliamentary assistant has said that he would permit this provision to be set aside until he obtains further information.

Could the parliamentary assistant tell the committee what the amount of this tax was previously? What was the amount of the retail purchase tax? I notice this change went into effect on March 23, 1949. Could he tell the committee whether,

on the basis on which it is now calculated, the tax is greater or smaller? Is there this pyramiding to which reference has been made, and if so is it more or less than it was before?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: To answer the earlier questions of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and the hon. member for Peterborough West, the Excise Tax Act makes provision that the tax shall not apply to railwaymen's watches, the purchase of which is authorized by the divisional superintendent of any railway; watches designed for the use of the blind; and alarm clocks sold at not more than $10 each.
Yes, but the cheap watch which sells at $2 or $3 is taxed. They are good watches, made in Canada-the best watches money can buy. In many instances they will outlast a 17-jewel watch.
Where are they made?

I do not hesitate for one moment to say that they are made in Peterborough by a firm the name of which I shall not mention. I can say however that more than 5,000 watches and clocks are turned out each day, the great majority of which are in the low-price field.
As the parliamentary assistant has said, the tax was first imposed at a 25 per cent rate, not for the purpose of collecting revenue, but only to stop the sale of these watches and clocks. We find however that the 10 per cent tax is retained. Why? People are now demanding these watches because the manufacture of them was held up during the war.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
While the tax has not been removed, there has been a substantial reduction in taxation in this group from 25 per cent to 10 per cent. The main purpose of tax reduction is to afford a measure of tax relief across the entire scale. I imagine each hon. member could build up a special case for special consideration of a certain industry in his riding. But the government has to look at the broad picture.
Turning to the question asked by the hon. member for Vancouver East, there will be a revenue loss of $8 million in this change from a 25 per cent retail tax to a 10 per cent excise tax at the manufacturers' level. I would point out that there will also be a very considerable saving in administrative cost, because it will be recalled that one of the difficulties of administering a retail sales tax arises from the great number of outlets which have to be supervised by the Department of National Revenue. In these jewelry shops there were some goods which were not taxable and others which were taxable
Excise Tax Act
at different rates. Now, if we have this tax tidied up and placed at 10 per cent at the manufacturers' level, the actual cost of administering the collection would be much less.

When the 10 per cent tax is placed at the manufacturers' level, and the sale is made to a jobber or wholesaler, how is the wholesaler's profit considered? Is not the tax taken into consideration, so that the wholesaler pays more than the 10 per cent? And when it comes to the retailer there is another addition. What tax does the retailer now pay?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Whether the jobber and wholesaler and retailer take today the same mark-up on the price they get from the manufacturer would depend upon their trade practice. But mathematically, even though they had, for example, a 50 per cent mark-up on the $1.10 they would now pay for an article now worth $1, still in the end when they take their usual mark-up there is only a 10 per cent increase in the actual retail price.
No, no.
No.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I can speak with some authority, because I remember when the former member for Beauce, who was a manufacturer, made this very argument. If the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar will follow through he will find that the actual 10 per cent increase at the manufacturers' level, if passed on by a mark-up, is still at 10 per cent increase in the final retail price. And that, of course, is the reason for the $8 million loss in revenue.
No.

No. The tax was formerly 25 per cent when the purchase was made in a retail store. The retailer therefore paid 25 per cent on the retail price. But here we have a 10 per cent tax at the manufacturers' level. The manufacturer sells it to the jobber, the jobber has that 10 per cent; it is then pyramided, and he sells it-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No.
Absolutely.

It jumps up; that is added to his price. He sells it to someone else-the wholesaler-and the wholesaler has to absorb the first 10 per cent, the write-up by the jobber. The wholesaler has it; he makes that addition, and it is sold to the retailer, and he has to add his profit with the pyramided 10 per cent, all the way up the line. The poor little fellow who has to buy the watch because he has not enough money to buy anything

Excise Tax Act
else has to pay it. He has to pay that pyramided price, which is not 10 per cent. The parliamentary assistant has the financial adviser and the deputy minister in front of him and I am sure they will tell him that the retailer is still paying close to 25 per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Let me take an actual example and follow it through and then I think the hon. gentleman will see that the ten per cent tax is still ten per cent on the retail end. Take an article which sells for one dollar at the manufacturing end. Assume that there is a markup of 100 per cent between the manufacturer and the retailer. It would sell at retail for $2. The previous tax was 25 per cent, so in that case the selling price would be $2.50. Take this 10 per cent excise tax on the $1. That would make it $1.10 at the wholesale end. The jobber and the middleman would still take a total of 100 per cent markup, making the final selling price $2.20. The price of $2.20 is 10 per cent, which is 30 cents less than the old price of $2.50.

I think we are talking at cross purposes. We are talking about the 10 per cent on the original dollar which is carried through instead of collecting 10 per cent from the retailer. It makes a great deal of difference with the same markup. We are suggesting that if we are going to have this tax, it should not be a hidden tax. It should be collected from the final purchaser. When you have all the markups you get a much different result.
The government will now get 10 per cent on the dollar, but under the other plan the purchaser would be paying only the 10 per cent. With all the markups right through to the retailer it is quite different.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If the tax was added at the manufacturing level or at the retailing level, it would still be selling for $1 and the markup would still make it $2 at the retailing level. A 10 per cent retail tax on the $2 would still make it $2.20, which is exactly the same.
The purchaser is paying 20 per cent on the original dollar.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Ten per cent on the retail price of $2.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: May I suggest that all hon. members who desire to ask questions should ask them and then the parliamentary assistant could reply at one time.

Perhaps if the parliamentary assistant would wait a moment until we have completed our questions we could make more headway. I think there has been some confusion of thought and terms in this discussion.
It is quite true that, where a tax is pyramided as an article is passed on through various hands, you still have in the end only the original tax; there is no increase in the tax. But when the purchase takes place after the final change of hands the purchaser is paying at least a markup on the tax plus a markup on the markup on the tax. If there happen to be four hands through which the article passes he would be paying also a markup on the markup on the markup on the tax.
The same process applies in the case of the sales tax. I cited an actual case to the house two years ago of a pair of stockings, where the 8 per cent sales tax is levied on the manufacturer. The manufacturer sells the stockings to the wholesaler who applies his markup, not just on the selling price to him but on the eight per cent tax as well. Then the article is passed on to the retailer, or there may be a jobber in between. Each adds his markup, and when a purchaser buys the goods over the counter he is paying the original tax, plus the wholesaler's 10 per cent markup on the tax, plus the retailer's 50 per cent markup on the markup on the tax.
In that simple case the amount paid by the purchaser was not eight per cent, it was 14-8 per cent. That does not mean that the government got 14-8 per cent; the government got only the eight per cent on the manufacturer's price, but the purchaser was paying 14-8 per cent. As long as the government continues to levy these excise taxes at the manufacturer's level the final purchaser is going to be paying the tax plus the markup on the tax plus the markup on the markup on the tax, and in some cases also a markup on the markup on the markup on the tax.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow we will continue in committee of ways and means to discuss the budget resolutions.
